Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Michael is a 26-year-old European-American man who works as a fisherman and is married. His recent experiences have been significantly impacted by trauma he experienced through torture. The vivid memories of that event continue to haunt him, particularly triggered by auditory cues such as the sounds of babies or public transport like buses. One day while out fishing with his crew, Michael’s phone buzzed with an unexpected ringtone—a sound similar to a baby crying. This simple noise immediately transported him back to the traumatic experience. He felt rage building within him and his body reenacted the physical sensations he had endured during the torture. The pain was so intense that it was as if the event were happening all over again. This intrusive memory left him feeling both physically and emotionally vulnerable, a state he now dreads. Michael’s sense of threat has become increasingly acute since these memories began to surface. He is certain that his back must be against a wall where he can see everything around him; otherwise, he feels unsafe. This constant vigilance extends beyond just his home environment—he notices potential weapons or dangerous objects wherever he goes. The fear of being in a vulnerable position again has made him hypervigilant and constantly scanning for any signs of danger. The memories that surface often lead to heightened states of threat perception. For instance, while riding the bus to town one day, the sound of squeaking brakes triggered another episode where Michael was transported back to his traumatic experience. The pain recall brought tears to his eyes and a deep sense of rage overwhelmed him as he clung to the seat, feeling trapped and vulnerable. This memory intensified his threat monitoring; he started listening more intently for any sounds that might indicate someone entering his home. The cycle has become self-reinforcing, with triggers leading to memories which then fuel his perception of threat, and this heightened sense of danger further reinforces the potency of the initial triggers. Michael’s occupation as a fisherman exacerbates this dynamic because he often works in isolated environments where he cannot control who might be around him or what dangers may arise. His marriage has also been affected by these changes. He avoids going to places that could potentially expose him to triggers, leading to social isolation and strained relationships with his spouse. The fear of feeling vulnerable again and the constant threat monitoring have made it difficult for Michael to engage in everyday activities without experiencing intense distress. What brought Michael to seek help was a particularly severe episode at work when he had an acute memory triggered by a noise similar to that heard on public transport. He felt immobilized, unable to continue his duties, and realized he needed support to manage these overwhelming experiences. His greatest fear is reliving the trauma through memories and feeling vulnerable again without any control over the situation. Michael hopes for relief from the constant state of threat monitoring and a return to a sense of safety in his daily life. He wants to be able to engage fully with his work and family without the paralyzing grip of past experiences controlling him.
